core_territory: Iraq's Kurdistan Region (KRI) — Erbil, Duhok and Sulaymaniyah governorates, plus Halabja (⚠️ KRI-membership date/status not independently confirmed this pass, see subdivisions.csv's own note on that row). Autonomous since 1991 (de facto) / 2005 (constitutional) — the one fully settled Kurdish case of the four.
domain_territory: Turkey: the 16 provinces flagged Kurdish-majority/plurality or mixed in subdivisions.csv (Adıyaman, Ağrı, Bingöl, Bitlis, Diyarbakır, Hakkâri, Mardin, Muş, Siirt, Batman, Şırnak, Van, Şanlıurfa, plus mixed Kars/Iğdır and the distinctively Zaza-speaking/Alevi Tunceli) — roughly half of all Kurds (frameworks survey §3.1). Iran: Kurdistan, Kermanshah and Ilam provinces (Kurdish-majority) plus West Azerbaijan (mixed Kurdish/Azeri) — 6-7 million people. Syria: Al-Hasakah and (partially) Raqqa governorates, the former Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria (AANES/'Rojava') territory, formally dissolved and integrated into the Syrian state 20 August 2026 (frameworks survey §3.4) — roughly 2.5 million people.
sphere_territory: (none named beyond the four host countries — Kurdish population also exists in the Caucasus and a global diaspora, outside this survey's scope)
confidence: high (Iraq's KRI legal status; the ~45 million/four-way population split); medium (Turkey's PKK ceasefire durability — the survey's own flag, since 1 March 2025; Syria's post-dissolution Kurdish status — also the survey's own flag, 20 August 2026); low (Iran — the survey explicitly names this 'the least researched' of the four, §3.6)
notes: ⚠️ THE SINGLE MOST STRUCTURALLY COMPLEX SPHERE IN THIS PACKAGE — read frameworks survey §3.7 before drawing anything. The survey explicitly declines to propose a treatment: 'a sphere overlay across all four host countries, per-country autonomous-region treatment matching each country's own real status, or something else' are all left open, with the explicit caution that Turkey's ceasefire or Syria's integration could still change again before a map is drawn. This file's core/domain split reflects only Iraq's settled legal autonomy as 'core' — it is not a claim about relative population weight or political legitimacy, the same disclaimer the mainland Southeast Asia package's S2 (Isan) note makes for its own core/domain convention.

core_territory: Iran (the region's major Shia power by reputation and self-identification — population share not independently re-verified this pass, per frameworks survey §4.2's own flag; treated as very-high-confidence background only). Iraq's Shia-majority governorates specifically — Basra, Dhi Qar, Maysan, Muthanna, Najaf, Karbala, Babil, Al-Qadisiyyah and Wasit — within an overall 65-70% Shia-majority country; Najaf and Karbala are also two of Shia Islam's holiest pilgrimage cities (frameworks survey §4.2).
domain_territory: Bahrain (~50% Shia population under a Sunni monarchy — 'a real, documented, structural tension,' §4.2). Lebanon's South and Baalbek-Hermel governorates (part of the country's 28% Shia population, one of three constitutionally-recognized confessional blocs, §4.3). Yemen's Houthi-held north (the Zaydi Shia tradition specifically, the Houthi movement's own religious base, ~35% of the national population, §5.4 — see subdivisions.csv for the current, live Houthi/PLC control split, which does not track this sectarian-geography line exactly). Syria's Latakia and Tartus governorates (historic Alawite heartland — a Shia-offshoot sect per §4.1 — combined with Twelver Shia at 15-20% nationally; the Assad family itself was Alawite). Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province (a real but unquantified Shia minority, sitting directly on the Ghawar oil field and the material survey's own core hydrocarbon geography — §4.2 and material survey §1.1).
sphere_territory: (none — this is a demographic-distribution layer entirely within this package's own countries, not a reach beyond it)
confidence: high (Iraq, Bahrain, Lebanon, Yemen and Syria figures — converging sources per the survey's own §4.2 table); ⚠️ explicitly NOT researched this pass for Iran or Saudi Arabia's exact population shares (the survey's own flag, §4.2) — both of those two rows rest on reputational/background-fact confidence only, not a sourced percentage.
notes: ⚠️ The frameworks survey explicitly 'takes no position on whether or how sectarian geography should inform any future map-data decision' (§4.4) — the same posture East Asia took toward the Hakka and Maritime Southeast Asia took toward Maluku's Christian/Muslim line. This file's core/domain split is drawn purely on population-share magnitude (majority vs. a significant, structurally-tense minority), not as any claim about political alignment, a bloc, or an 'axis' — Iran's and Iraq's Shia populations are not politically unified with Lebanon's, Yemen's or Bahrain's, and this sphere should be drawn, if drawn at all, as a demographic-geography layer only. This is the single most sensitive judgment call in this package — treat it with the same caution the frameworks survey itself uses. Lebanon's confessional constitution (§4.3 — president Maronite Christian, PM Sunni, speaker of parliament Shia by law, not just custom) is a genuinely distinctive governance structure with no equivalent elsewhere in this survey's scope and may deserve its own separate flag beyond this sphere, not folded silently into it.

core_territory: Turkey (all 81 provinces) — Turkish is a Turkic language, part of the same language family as Kazakh, Uzbek, Turkmen and Kyrgyz (frameworks survey §7.3).
domain_territory: (none within this package's own country set — Turkey is this sphere's sole member inside the Middle East/Turkey/Afghanistan map)
sphere_territory: Labeled only, drawn on the companion Central Asia map instead, not here: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Kyrgyzstan (all four Central Asia map-data package nations, whose titular languages are Turkic) — the same cross-map-connector convention the mainland/maritime Southeast Asia packages established with their own S5 'Patani Malay World' link. Azerbaijan is also named by the survey as geographically adjacent and linguistically Turkic but sits outside both this project's Middle East and Central Asia country scopes entirely — label only if a map's extent reaches that far, draw no territory for it.
confidence: medium — the frameworks survey's own words: 'a genuine cross-region sphere-overlay candidate... not proposed as settled geometry here, only flagged as available and well-grounded.'
notes: The real, current institutional expression is the Organization of Turkic States — named by the survey but 'not independently researched this pass, flagged as a natural next step' (§7.3). This is the first of this package's two cross-map connectors to `../central-asia-map-data/` (see S4 below for the second) — the same shape of link the mainland/maritime Southeast Asia packages already established; see that pair's own spheres.csv for the working precedent if useful.

core_territory: Afghanistan (all 34 provinces) — its Tajik (25-27% of the population, concentrated north/northeast/the Kabul region), Uzbek (6-15%, north) and Turkmen (1.5-3%) populations are, per the frameworks survey, 'ethnically and linguistically the same peoples as the titular nationalities of three of the companion Central Asia survey's five countries... not a distant cultural echo but a direct population continuity split by a modern border' (§7.4). Afghanistan's official Dari language is also a Persian-family language, giving the country a second real tie — to Iran's own Persian/Iranic core — distinct from its Central Asian ethnic ties.
domain_territory: Iran (Persian/Farsi-speaking core provinces, mutually intelligible with Afghan Dari) — the Persian/Iranic half of Afghanistan's own 'two bridges.'
sphere_territory: Labeled only, drawn on the companion Central Asia map instead: Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan specifically (the Turkic/Tajik-Persianate half of Afghanistan's two bridges) — per the frameworks survey's own explicit flag (§7.4), Afghanistan 'may be this region's single strongest argument for treating West Asia as one connected map-data space rather than two entirely separate ones,' since its population ties run in both directions the survey's own Central Asia/Middle East split otherwise keeps apart.
confidence: medium — Afghanistan's overall ethnic percentages are sourced with wide ranges ('estimates vary by source') per the survey's own table; the specific cross-border population-continuity claim is the survey's own stated reasoning, not an independently re-verified figure this pass.
notes: ⚠️ The frameworks survey explicitly did NOT research the current Taliban government's structure or its relationship to this ethnic breakdown (§7.4) — a real, flagged gap, 'given how load-bearing ethnic-composition-versus-governing-group tension has been to nearly every other stateless/sub-state-nation case in this survey.' This is this package's SECOND cross-map connector to `../central-asia-map-data/`, alongside S3's Pan-Turkic sphere — the two together are why the frameworks survey itself suggests the two halves of West Asia might eventually be considered one connected map space rather than two, a scoping question left for the author, not decided here.
